profiles.name: Joe Silver
profiles.excerpt: Joe Silver brought one of show business's deepest voices from Broadway into television, film and the repertory of CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Joe Silver was born in Chicago in 1922 and grew up in Green Bay, Wisconsin. He made his Broadway debut in a 1942 revival of Tobacco Road and developed into a durable stage character actor, eventually earning a Tony Award nomination for playing multiple roles in Lenny.

Silver's exceptionally deep voice made him equally distinctive away from the stage. He worked extensively in television, film and voiceover and became a recurring member of CBS Radio Mystery Theater, where a voice with that much weight could suggest menace, authority or comedy before a character had said more than a few lines.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 27 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Silver, documenting the radio-drama side of a career that stretched across nearly five decades.

profiles.name: Leo Curley
profiles.excerpt: Leo Curley was a dependable western-radio character actor whose surviving GRH work is concentrated in Wild Bill Hickok and Roy Rogers.
profiles.bio_html:
Leo Curley worked in the professional western repertory that supplied network radio with lawmen, ranchers, townsmen and outlaws from week to week. Personal biography survives only in fragments, but cast records place him repeatedly in major western programs during the early 1950s.

Curley appeared alongside Guy Madison and Andy Devine on The Adventures of Wild Bill Hickok and also worked on The Roy Rogers Show. Earlier radio histories identify him with western serial work stretching back to the era of Tom Mix, giving his microphone career deeper roots than the surviving GRH holdings alone suggest.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 Wild Bill Hickok performances credited to Curley, five Roy Rogers appearances, two Tales of the Texas Rangers episodes and additional work on Fibber McGee and Molly, Gunsmoke and Lux Radio Theatre.

profiles.name: Michael Wager
profiles.excerpt: Michael Wager brought a serious New York stage career into radio, becoming a recurring CBS Radio Mystery Theater actor after Broadway and film work.
profiles.bio_html:
Michael Wager was born Emanuel Weisgal in New York City in 1925. He established himself in the theatre during the 1950s, appearing on Broadway in productions including Bernardine, The Merchant of Venice, Saint Joan and The Firstborn, while also working in film and television.

Wager's stage discipline translated naturally to microphone drama. During the 1970s he became a recurring performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, joining the New York repertory that supplied the series with actors capable of moving quickly among literary, supernatural and contemporary roles.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 27 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Wager. Those broadcasts document a substantial radio chapter within a career otherwise remembered primarily for theatre, film and television.

profiles.name: Tom McKee
profiles.excerpt: Tom McKee combined radio announcing with character acting before moving into film and television, leaving a strong GRH record in western and literary drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Tom McKee was born in New York City in 1917 and grew up in Buffalo. By 1940 he was already working professionally as a radio announcer, giving him a microphone background before acting became the more visible side of his career.

McKee later worked extensively as a character actor in radio, film and television. His radio credits include western drama, musical anthology and literary adaptation, while screen audiences later saw him on programs such as Maverick, Cheyenne and Tales of Wells Fargo. His earlier announcing work remains a genuine second professional branch.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Tales of the Texas Rangers performances credited to McKee, seven The Railroad Hour appearances, six NBC University Theater broadcasts, two Let George Do It episodes and additional work on Barrie Craig and Rocky Fortune.

profiles.name: Adele Jergens
profiles.excerpt: Adele Jergens carried a successful film career into radio as Carol Curtis, the sharp-witted partner to Glenn Langan's crime reporter on Stand By for Crime.
profiles.bio_html:
Adele Jergens was born in Brooklyn in 1917 and entered entertainment through modeling, dance and stage work. She performed as a Rockette, worked as a model and showgirl, and signed with Columbia Pictures in the 1940s, becoming a familiar blonde character actress in crime pictures, comedies and musicals.

Radio paired Jergens with her real-life husband Glenn Langan on the syndicated crime series Stand By for Crime. Langan played radio newscaster Chuck Morgan while Jergens played Carol Curtis, his capable companion in investigations that repeatedly pulled the pair from the studio into murder and criminal intrigue.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 26 Stand By for Crime performances credited to Jergens. The series gives her radio career a clear continuing role rather than a collection of isolated guest appearances.

profiles.name: Raymond Lawrence
profiles.excerpt: Raymond Lawrence was a British-born character actor whose radio work ranged from literary adaptation to suspense and feature-film dramatization.
profiles.bio_html:
Raymond Lawrence was born in London in 1888 and built a long acting career across stage and screen before radio became another outlet for his character work. His screen credits stretch from the 1930s into the postwar period, reflecting a professional life already well established before many of his surviving broadcasts.

Radio used Lawrence across literary adaptations, suspense and prestige drama. He appeared repeatedly on NBC University Theater and Escape, two programs that demanded clarity and control from supporting actors working with dense scripts and highly atmospheric production.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten NBC University Theater performances credited to Lawrence, eight Escape appearances, six Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and additional work on Suspense and The Halls of Ivy.

profiles.name: Alice Reinheart
profiles.excerpt: Alice Reinheart was a major old-time radio actress whose career combined stage training, musical ability and a broad repertory of mystery and dramatic roles.
profiles.bio_html:
Alice Reinheart was born in San Francisco in 1910 and showed early talent in music, giving piano concerts while still a child before studying journalism, drama, languages and music. She began professional stage work in stock theatre as a teenager and reached Broadway in the early 1930s.

Radio became one of the central parts of Reinheart's career. She worked in serials, mystery programs and anthology drama and became known for the versatility that allowed her to move from sympathetic leads to darker suspense roles. Her later television career extended that same character range into a new medium.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances credited to Reinheart, eight The Whistler appearances, two each on Quiet, Please and This Is Your FBI, and additional work on I Love a Mystery, Let George Do It, Molle Mystery Theatre and The Clock.

profiles.name: Anne Seymour
profiles.excerpt: Anne Seymour was one of radio drama's leading actresses, starring for years as Mary Marlin and continuing into mystery and anthology radio across several decades.
profiles.bio_html:
Anne Seymour was born in New York City in 1909 into a theatrical family and trained for the stage before making her radio debut in Cincinnati in 1932. She quickly became one of network radio's most experienced dramatic actresses.

Seymour's major continuing roles included Mary Marlin on The Story of Mary Marlin and Prudence Dane on A Woman of America. Her work also extended through serials, anthology drama and mystery programs, and she remained active long enough to appear in later revival series such as Theater Five and CBS Radio Mystery Theater.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances credited to Seymour, five CBS Radio Mystery Theater appearances, four Quiet, Please episodes, two each on Theater Five, Words at War and X Minus One, plus additional work on Lights Out and Sears Radio Theater.

profiles.name: Ben Morris
profiles.excerpt: Ben Morris briefly took over the title role in Pat Novak, for Hire and also worked in the eerie ensemble of Dark Fantasy, giving him two very different radio identities.
profiles.bio_html:
Ben Morris was a radio actor whose surviving work connects two distinct corners of 1940s broadcasting. He appeared in the Oklahoma City-produced supernatural anthology Dark Fantasy and later stepped into one of hard-boiled radio's most distinctive title roles.

When Jack Webb left the original West Coast run of Pat Novak, for Hire, Morris succeeded him as waterfront troubleshooter Pat Novak during 1947. The role required the same clipped, cynical narration and tough dialogue that defined the series, placing Morris at the center of the program rather than in a supporting repertory part.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 21 Dark Fantasy performances credited to Morris and four Pat Novak, for Hire broadcasts, preserving both his ensemble horror work and his period as the series' leading detective.
